# The Cartography of Almost

There's a map I keep in my mind that doesn't correspond to any real geography. It's made entirely of near-misses — moments where things were almost different. I can trace its borders with my eyes closed.

There's the intersection in Portland where I almost turned left instead of right. There's the handwritten note I almost sent. There's the job I almost accepted, which would have moved me to a city I'd never visited, where I'd have married someone I'd never met, or maybe I'd have stayed alone and lonely and discovered a different version of myself, one who played saxophone or collected antique typewriters or learned to make bread.

We spend so much energy on the roads taken that we forget the weight of the roads not taken is equally real. Not taken doesn't mean nonexistent. It means the branch is still growing in an alternate forest, and somewhere in that forest, a version of you is standing still, listening to leaves fall, wondering what it would have been like to have been braver.

I think about this a lot because I'm the kind of person who says "I should have" the way other people breathe — constantly, without noticing, without concern. I should have stayed in bed. I should have called. I should have said the thing while the thing was still sayable.

The past tense is a cruel grammatical construction. It locks doors that were never meant to be permanent. It gives finality to chapters that were still being written, and yet we trust it. We trust it the way we trust anything repeated often enough — not because it's true, but because it's familiar.

I once read that memory is not a recording but a reconstruction — that every time you remember something, you're actually building it again, slightly differently, with slightly different furniture in the room, a slightly different light through the window. If this is true, then nostalgia is a kind of authorship. We're not revisiting our lives. We're rewriting them. Every single time. And the version we end up loving — the warm autumn afternoon, the perfect first date, the golden hour on the beach — might never have existed at all. It might just be the edit.

This should terrify us, but it doesn't. Instead it comforts us, because the implication is that the past can be edited still. We can always revise. We can always make it softer, blur the edges, remove the painful scenes, replace the dialogue with something we wish we'd said.

But the present doesn't offer this luxury. The present is being written as you read this, and the words aren't clear yet. They're wet ink on paper, smudging if you touch them too soon. You can't edit what you haven't finished. You can only squint and hope and keep your hand steady.

I think about what it would feel like to live without that squint — to stop trying to read the future before it's legible. To just exist inside the sentence of this moment without peeking ahead at the period. Some people manage this. They seem to occupy time differently, like they've found a door in the ordinary hour and slipped through into somewhere that doesn't have a clock. They talk about being present as if it's a skill, which it probably is, but I suspect it's also a kind of courage, because presence means accepting that you don't know what's coming, and that you can't do anything about what already came.

There's a Japanese word — *mono no aware* — that describes the gentle sadness of things passing. Not a grief, exactly. Not even sorrow. Something softer. The way you feel when cherry blossoms fall, or when a song you love ends and you sit in the silence for a moment before reaching for the remote. It's the awareness that beauty and impermanence are the same thing. That the flower is beautiful because it's dying. That you'll only get so many seasons.

I want to learn that. Not the philosophy — anyone can read the philosophy. I want to learn the feeling. I want to be the kind of person who watches the petals fall and thinks *yes, this is how it's supposed to be* rather than *why can't they stay*.

But I'm not there yet. Right now, I'm still the person who replays conversations. Still the one who draws maps of almost. Still the one who stands at intersections and feels the ghost of an alternate life brushing past like a stranger's sleeve.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe the honest version of a life isn't the one lived without regret, but the one lived with enough awareness to notice what nearly was. Maybe the near-misses are what give the hits their meaning. You can't feel the sharpness of where you are without occasionally tracing the smooth outline of where you aren't.

So I'll keep the map. I'll fold it carefully and put it in my pocket. I'll pull it out sometimes, in quiet moments, and look at all the roads that don't exist. And then I'll unfold myself again, right here, in this room, in this hour that is already passing, and I'll try — not perfectly, not effortlessly, but try — to be where my feet are.

The ink is still wet. I'd better keep moving before it smudges.
